questions.q: What is the effect of updating a flawed account rule on transactions that were already accounted under the old version?
options: It automatically corrects every previously accounted transaction retroactively
It permanently deletes all previously accounted transactions
It has no effect on anything, including future transactions
It does nothing to those transactions by itself; the fix only changes how future Create Accounting runs behave
questions.explain: Correcting a rule changes future behavior only; transactions already accounted under the old rule retain whatever that old rule produced until separately corrected.

questions.q: What is the correct approach for affected transactions that are still in Draft status?
options: They cannot be corrected at all
They must be manually deleted from the database
Simply re-run Create Accounting in Draft mode, which cleanly applies the corrected rule and replaces the old result
They require a General Ledger period-close adjustment
questions.explain: Draft entries can be safely re-created; re-running Create Accounting in Draft mode applies the corrected rule and replaces the prior draft result.

questions.q: Why is correcting already-Final, not-yet-transferred entries more sensitive than correcting Draft entries?
options: It isn't more sensitive; both are handled identically
Because Final entries do not actually exist in the database
Because Draft entries require more approvals than Final entries
Because Final entries cannot simply be deleted or silently altered, requiring a reversal-and-re-entry approach instead, applied to every affected transaction
questions.explain: Final entries require reversal rather than deletion or silent alteration, and this needs to be applied to every transaction the flawed rule affected.

questions.q: What additional consideration applies to affected transactions that have already been transferred to GL and posted?
options: No additional consideration; subledger-level correction alone is always sufficient
They can be ignored entirely since GL balances cannot be wrong
Correcting them also touches the General Ledger, requiring the company's period-close and adjustment procedures to be followed, not just subledger-level reversal
Only Oracle Support can correct a posted GL entry
questions.explain: Once transactions are transferred and posted in GL, correction must also respect GL's own period-close and adjustment procedures, on top of subledger reversal.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize determining the full scope of affected transactions before correcting anything?
options: Scope does not matter; correcting just one transaction is always sufficient
Because Oracle automatically identifies every affected transaction without any reporting
Because scope only matters for Draft transactions, never for Final ones
Because correcting only the one transaction that was noticed, while leaving other equally affected transactions untouched, leaves the books still wrong, just less visibly so
questions.explain: A flawed rule often affects more than just the one transaction that happened to be noticed; the Account Analysis Report and Journal Entries Report help identify the complete affected population.
